title: Quantization technical review - Verdant AI
summary: Redwood SE team reviewed INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ tradeoffs for Verdant's LLM inference stack. Main concerns: accuracy regressions on instruction-following tasks, tail latencies with batching+KV cache, and VPC/on-prem integration for PII data. Agreed next steps: run a 1k-prompt benchmark on Verdant sample set with AWQ and GPTQ variants, share quantization guide and perf spreadsheet, and schedule POC with Dedicated nodes in their VPC.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-10
Start time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Verdant CTO), Priya Rao (Verdant ML Eng), Sam Bennett (Verdant Infra), Nadia Chen (Verdant Security)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros? we'll use this time to deep dive on quantization options and runtime tradeoffs. Maya and Diego from our SE team will lead the tech bits.
[00:18] Liam: yea thanks, liam here. we looked at the doc you sent. main ask is: can we get to ~2x cost reduction without losing instruction-following quality for our 13B model family. also must satisfy our VPC/on-prem constraints for PII.
[00:34] Maya: cool, that is helpful. quick clarifying q: when you say 13B family, is that a native fp16 baseline you run today? and what's your current batch sizes/latency targets?
[00:45] Priya: currently fp16 on A100-ish on prem; 9 to 12 token/sec roughly per stream, target p50 latency < 200ms for short prompts (<= 256 tokens), and avg batch sizes depend but around 4-8 for live API.
[01:05] Diego: perfect. so we typically evaluate INT8, FP8, GPTQ and AWQ style methods. each has tradeoffs: INT8 can give good perf but requires careful per-channel quant and outlier handling; FP8 maintains more dynamic range but needs specialized kernels and sometimes compiler support.
[01:28] Priya: quick interjection - we've seen accuracy regressions in prior runs with naively applied GPTQ, especially on instruction-following evals. is that expected?
[01:39] Maya: yes, totally. GPTQ (we sometimes say G P T Q in notes) compresses weights post-hoc and can cause small calibration shifts. AWQ is a newer algorithm that handles activation-aware quant better for transformer layers, often reducing regresses on sensitive prompts, but it's not a silver bullet.
[01:58] Liam: can you say more about where regressions come from? per-layer sensitivity? attention vs feedforward?
[02:07] Diego: mostly yes - some layers are more sensitive, especially final projection and certain MLP layers where outliers dominate. per-block mixed-precision (keep sensitive layers in fp16) is common. we also see tokenization differences when logits shift slightly which cascades in instruction tasks.
[02:29] [02:30] Jordan: side note - on runtime side, kernel selection matters: our runtime will pick optimized kernels based on sequence length and model layout. for AWQ/GPTQ we route to quantized kernels; fallback to fp16 for chosen layers if accuracy drops.
[02:47] Sam: what about KV cache and batching? our workload is lots of short chats so KV cache hit rate matters and we worry about tail latency when big batches pile up.
[02:59] Maya: good point. continuous batching helps throughput but increases tail latency. we do workload-aware batching where we cap batch formation window and prioritize low-latency routes. KV cache eviction policy can also impact perf: smaller KV cache reduces memory but increases recompute for long contexts.
[03:20] Priya: do quantized models use the same KV cache layout? any differences causing correctness issues?
[03:28] Diego: generally same logical KV cache; but quantized runtime might pack tensors differently in memory which can change memory footprint and slightly impact memory-bound kernels. correctness should be preserved; however serialization/deserialization between services (e.g., when routing to fallback model variant) needs careful dtype handling. we sometimes see typos in dtype casting leading to small numerical diffs.
[03:52] [04:00] Liam: how about FP8 - is that pragmatic for us? we run on-prem and some cloud dedicated fleets.
[04:08] Maya: FP8 promises faster compute vs fp16 for some hardware if kernels exist; but ecosystem support is spotty. plus you'd need tuned kernels (triton, cutlass) and sometimes compiler passes. FP8 can reduce memory but may require retraining or fine-tuning to hit parity on instruction tasks.
[04:28] Priya: what's Redwood's recommendation for a trial?
[04:33] Jordan: run parallel pipelines: GPTQ baseline, AWQ optimized, and an INT8 with selective fp16 layers. measure both quality on your instruction eval set and perf: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and memory headroom.
[04:50] Diego: we can run a 1k prompt bench across the sample set you gave. we will log per-prompt deltas (emd or bleu-ish proxies) and flag any prompts with >X% regression. also include log-prob shifts for calibration.
[05:10] Priya: what's a reasonable threshold for regression? we care about hallucination and instruction-following utility.
[05:18] Maya: common rule: <1-2% top-level metric drop is tolerable for many customers, but instruction tasks sometimes require stricter like <0.5%. we can help tune per-layer keep list to target that.
[05:35] Liam: what about kernel-level throughput: any numbers we can expect?
[05:40] Diego: approximate: for a 13B model on A100, fp16 might do X tokens/s, INT8 can get 1.6-2x depending on batch and sequence length. AWQ/GPTQ similar range but AWQ often has fewer accuracy regressions - so it's a trade. specific numbers depend on batch size, sequence length, and KV cache usage.
[06:03] [06:15] Sam: we need to run within our VPC. how does Redwood Private fit here? can we run quantized runtime in our network?
[06:23] Jordan: yes - Redwood Private deploys the control plane or compute as an appliance inside your VPC/on-prem. we support KMS integration for keys, and can run Dedicated with VPC-only endpoints. Diego: we'll provide an architecture diagram.
[06:40] Nadia: security question: do the quantized artifacts contain any PII? are snapshots or logs masked?
[06:48] Maya: quantized weights are model params; they don't contain training data or PII. runtime logs can be configured to redact prompts; our private deployment gives you full control over retention and audit logs. we support SAML/SSO, RBAC and KMS/HSM integrations.
[07:05] Priya: do you support on-the-fly reloading of model variants? we want canarying between fp16 and quantized versions.
[07:13] Diego: yes, rollouts supported - you can route a percentage of traffic to a variant. fallback policy can auto-shift traffic to fp16 if error rates or quality regressions spike.
[07:26] [07:30] Jordan: let's talk about calibration and outliers: GPTQ often requires per-channel scales and calibration with representative data. AWQ explicitly models activation distribution and handles outliers better.
[07:42] Priya: will we need to store extra metadata per model to support mixed precision?
[07:47] Maya: yes small metadata like keep-lists, per-layer scale tables. Redwood's model registry stores that alongside the model artifacts so serving runtime picks correct kernels and keep list.
[08:00] Liam: on perf benchmarking, what data will you need from us?
[08:06] Diego: sample eval set of 1k prompts representative of production, a few long-context cases (2-4), typical batch distribution, and a list of target p50/p95 latency SLOs. also your target throughput cost goals.
[08:20] Priya: we can provide that by EOD Monday.
[08:24] [08:30] Maya: great. on the runtime side also watch for tail latencies caused by shard imbalance - when using large batches with kv cache misses, some requests wait for straggler shards. our scheduler tries cross-shard batching and preemptive scheduling to limit tail.
[08:45] Liam: curious about memory for KV cache under quantized weights - any changes?
[08:49] Diego: KV cache stores activations (keys/values) in fp16 typically; quantized weights reduce parameter storage but KV cache size roughly unchanged. however total GPU memory footprint goes down with quant weights which can allow larger caches or bigger batches.
[09:04] [09:15] Priya: did we talk about retraining vs post-quantization? we prefer post-quant because we can't afford full retrain.
[09:20] Maya: post-quant is standard. some customers do small LoRA or fine-tune to recover edge-case regressions if needed. AWQ/GPTQ both post-quant; AWQ sometimes needs less fine-tune.
[09:34] Sam: licensing/licensing note - any IP or runtime limitations for AWQ?
[09:39] Jordan: AWQ implementations vary; some are community, some have licensing; we'll surface specifics in the guide.
[09:48] [10:00] Diego: operational notes: we monitor token-level cost and latency per-model per-route. for quant models we add a quality-monitor that tracks regressions on a sample evaluation set and alerts when thresholds cross.
[10:12] Priya: can you show example per-prompt regression output?
[10:16] Maya: yes we'll include a sample table in the spreadsheet showing per-prompt delta, log-prob shift, and actions (keep-list, fp16 fallback).
[10:26] Liam: what's typical time to produce quant artifacts for a 13B?
[10:30] Diego: end-to-end: with dedicated CPU/GPU worker it can be a few hours to run GPTQ/AWQ and validate for 13B, plus a tuning pass. if we queue on shared infra it could take longer.
[10:43] Priya: do quantized models require special container images?
[10:46] Maya: runtime images include quant kernels; we provide both standard and quant-optimized images. for Private you'll run our quant-optimized runtime in your env.
[10:55] [11:05] Jordan: okay let's capture next steps - we'll run the 1k bench, share artifacts, and schedule a POC kickoff.
[11:12] Nadia: we'll review security docs when you send them.
[11:15] Liam: anything else?
[11:18] Maya: one last note: watch for small numeric diffs - sometimes eval metrics won't capture user-visible regressions. recommend human spot checks on top failing prompts.
[11:30] Jordan: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the perf spreadsheet and data requests.

End of transcript.

Notes about transcription quality: Some speaker labels may be generic and there are occasional transcription errors (G P T Q spaced tokens, typos). Timestamps are approximated every 15-90 seconds.
questions: How do AWQ and GPTQ compare on instruction-following quality for 13B models?
What are the required artifacts and metrics for benchmarking quantized models in our VPC?
